title: Python Foundations
description: Learn programming by writing small, useful programs. Covers variables, logic, loops, functions, files, error handling, and a complete command-line project.

badge.name: Python Pioneer
badge.description: Awarded for completing Python Foundations and its final assessment.

outcomes: Write and run Python scripts from the command line
Store and transform data with variables, lists, and dictionaries
Use conditions, loops, and functions to structure programs
Read and write text files safely
Handle common errors and debug a failing program
Build a working command-line expense tracker
prerequisites: A computer with Python 3 installed (the course shows how to check).
A text editor or code editor such as VS Code.
tools: VS Code, Thonny, or another editor

modules.title: First steps
modules.summary: What Python is, how to run it, and the first few lines of real code.

content.text: Programming is the practice of writing precise instructions for a computer. Python is a popular language because its syntax is close to readable English.

A program takes input, does something with it, and produces output. A calculator takes numbers and an operation. A to-do list takes tasks and remembers them. Even a large application is built from small steps like these.

items: **Input:** data from a user, a file, a sensor, or another program.
**Processing:** calculations, comparisons, sorting, converting.
**Output:** text on screen, a saved file, a message, or a request.
**Control flow:** deciding which instructions run and how often.

content.title: You are learning a way of thinking
content.text: Syntax is the easy part. The durable skill is breaking a problem into steps small enough to test.

content.question: Which sequence describes a basic program?
content.explanation: Most programs can be understood as taking input, processing it, and producing output.

lessons.title: Install and run your first script

content.text: You do not need a complicated setup. A Python interpreter, a text file, and a terminal are enough to start.

Install Python 3 from python.org and make sure 'Add Python to PATH' is selected on Windows if you want the `python` command available in your terminal. On macOS and Linux, `python3` is usually the command.

content.code:
python --version
# or
python3 --version

mkdir python-practice
cd python-practice
code hello.py

print("Hello, Skillshop!")
name = input("What is your name? ")
print(f"Welcome, {name}.")

content.text: Save the file as `hello.py`, then run it with `python hello.py` or `python3 hello.py`. If the terminal prints a greeting and asks for your name, your setup works.

content.title: If the command is not found
content.text: Python may be installed but not on your PATH. Re-run the installer and select the PATH option, or use the full path to the Python executable. You can also run scripts from within your editor.

content.question: Which command usually runs a Python file on Windows after Python is added to PATH?
content.explanation: The Python interpreter is invoked with the script path.

content.text: A variable is a name for a value. Good names make the program understandable; bad names turn it into a puzzle.

Python creates a variable when you assign to it. The value can be a string, an integer, a decimal, a boolean, or a more complex object. Use `input()` to read text and convert it when you need a number.

content.code:
name = "Sam"
age = 28
hourly_rate = 18.50
is_active = True

user_name = input("Your name: ")
hours = float(input("Hours worked: "))
pay = hours * hourly_rate

print(f"{user_name} earned {pay:.2f} this week.")

content.title: Input always starts as text
content.text: `input()` returns a string. Convert with `int()` or `float()` before doing maths. If the user types letters, the conversion raises a ValueError, which you will handle later.

content.question: What type does input() return?
content.explanation: All user input is read as a string. Convert it explicitly when needed.

modules.title: Logic and control
modules.summary: Make decisions, repeat work, and package behaviour into functions.

content.text: Conditions let a program choose a path. Python evaluates a boolean expression and runs the matching block.
Comparison operators return True or False. Combine them with `and`, `or`, and `not`. Indentation is part of Python's syntax: the indented block belongs to the line above it.

rows: Greater or equal / less or equal
At least one condition must be true

content.title: = is assignment, == is comparison
content.text: `x = 5` stores 5. `x == 5` asks whether x is 5. Mixing them up is one of the first bugs everyone writes.

content.question: Which expression checks whether age is at least 18?
content.explanation: >= means greater than or equal to.

content.text: Loops repeat work. Use `for` when you know what you are iterating over, and `while` when you repeat until a condition changes.

A `for` loop walks through a sequence such as a list or a range of numbers. A `while` loop keeps going as long as a condition is true. Every `while` loop needs a route to becoming false, or it will run forever.

items: `range(5)` gives 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.
`range(1, 6)` gives 1 through 5. The end value is excluded.
`break` exits the nearest loop immediately.
`continue` skips to the next iteration.
`for...else` runs the `else` block only if the loop completed without `break`.

content.title: Beware the infinite loop
content.text: If a `while` condition never becomes false and there is no `break`, the program keeps running. Press Ctrl + C in the terminal to stop it.

content.question: How many numbers does range(1, 6) produce?
content.explanation: The stop value is excluded, so it yields 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.

content.text: A function gives a name to a reusable piece of logic. It takes inputs, does work, and optionally returns a result.

Define a function with `def`, give it parameters, and use `return` to send a value back. A function that only prints is doing output; a function that returns a value can be tested and reused more easily.

content.code:
def calculate_pay(hours, rate, overtime_after=40, overtime_rate=1.5):
    regular_hours = min(hours, overtime_after)
    overtime_hours = max(hours - overtime_after, 0)
    return regular_hours * rate + overtime_hours * rate * overtime_rate

weekly_pay = calculate_pay(45, 20)
print(f"Pay: {weekly_pay:.2f}")

content.text: Why return instead of print?

items: A returned value can be stored, compared, formatted, or passed to another function.
A function that prints is harder to reuse and test.
Default arguments make a function flexible without forcing every caller to supply every value.
Keep functions small enough to explain in one sentence.

content.title: Name functions with verbs
content.text: `calculate_pay`, `load_tasks`, and `format_name` describe actions. `pay` or `stuff` makes the caller guess.

content.question: What does return do in a function?
options: Prints a value to the screen
Sends a value back to the caller
content.explanation: Return ends the function and passes a value back to the code that called it.

modules.title: Collections and files
modules.summary: Store many values and keep them after the program closes.

content.text: A list is an ordered, changeable collection. Use it whenever you have many of the same kind of thing: tasks, scores, names, file paths.
Python lists are zero-indexed. `items[0]` is the first element. Negative indexes count from the end. Lists have methods for adding, removing, sorting, and counting.

content.code:
tasks = ["read", "write", "review"]
tasks.append("ship")
tasks.remove("read")

for index, task in enumerate(tasks, start=1):
    print(index, task)

print(tasks[0])      # first item
print(tasks[-1])     # last item
print(len(tasks))    # count

content.title: Tuples are for fixed groups
content.text: A tuple such as `(latitude, longitude)` is ordered and cannot be changed. Use a tuple when the values belong together and should not be individually replaced.

content.question: What is tasks[-1]?
content.explanation: Negative indexes count backwards from the end.

content.text: A dictionary stores named values. It is the natural structure for a record such as a product, a task, or a person.
Keys must be unique and hashable, often strings. Values can be anything. Access a key with square brackets, but use `.get()` when a missing key should not crash the program.
A list of dictionaries
Most real datasets are a list of dictionaries: each dictionary is a row, each key is a column. This is also the structure JSON uses, which makes it ideal for saving data to a file.

content.code:
expenses = [
    {"category": "food", "amount": 24.00},
    {"category": "transport", "amount": 12.50},
    {"category": "food", "amount": 9.75}
]

total = sum(item["amount"] for item in expenses)
print(f"Total: {total:.2f}")

content.title: Use .get() for optional fields
content.text: `expense["receipt"]` raises a KeyError if the key is missing. `expense.get("receipt", "none")` returns a safe default.

content.question: Which structure best represents a list of records with named fields?
content.explanation: Each dictionary can hold named fields, and the list holds the rows.

content.text: Files let data survive after the program ends. Use the `with open(...)` pattern so Python closes the file even if something fails.

Text files are simple and portable. JSON is excellent for structured lists and dictionaries. Use `json.dump()` to write and `json.load()` to read. Always handle the case where the file does not exist yet.

content.code:
import json
from pathlib import Path

path = Path("expenses.json")

def load_expenses(path):
    if not path.exists():
        return []
    with path.open("r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        return json.load(file)

def save_expenses(path, expenses):
    with path.open("w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        json.dump(expenses, file, indent=2)

expenses = load_expenses(path)
expenses.append({"category": "food", "amount": 15.50})
save_expenses(path, expenses)
print("Saved", len(expenses), "expenses.")

items: Use `"r"` to read, `"w"` to overwrite, and `"a"` to append.
Specify `encoding="utf-8"` for predictable text.
Validate loaded data before assuming it has the expected keys.
Write to a temporary file first if a crash mid-save would be costly.
Never trust a path supplied by a user without checking it.

content.title: Opening in write mode erases the file
content.text: `open(path, "w")` truncates an existing file as soon as it opens. Load first if you intend to keep old data.

content.question: Which pattern ensures a file is closed even if an exception occurs?
content.explanation: The with statement manages closing automatically.

modules.title: Working like a programmer
modules.summary: Modules, errors, environments, and the habits that make code maintainable.

content.text: Python ships with a large standard library. Before writing a utility from scratch, check whether it already exists.
Import a module with `import` and use its names with a dot. You can import specific functions with `from module import function`. Give imports meaningful names only when it improves clarity.

content.code:
from datetime import date, timedelta
from pathlib import Path
import random

print(date.today())
print(date.today() + timedelta(days=7))
print(Path.cwd())
print(random.choice(["rock", "paper", "scissors"]))

content.title: Standard library first
content.text: A package on the internet may be excellent, but every dependency is something to install, update, and trust. Use the standard library when it solves the problem cleanly.

content.question: Which module helps you work with filesystem paths?
content.explanation: pathlib provides an object-oriented way to handle paths and files.

content.text: An exception is not a moral failure. It is information about where the program's assumptions broke.

Read the traceback from the bottom up: the final line tells you the error type and message, and the lines above tell you the call path. Catch only the errors you can actually handle, and print or log enough context to understand what happened.

items: Read the last line of the traceback first.
Reproduce the bug with the smallest possible input.
Print or inspect variable values just before the failure.
Use `python -m pdb script.py` or your editor's debugger to step through code.
Write a tiny test that fails, then fix it.
Avoid bare `except:` blocks; they hide unexpected errors.

content.title: Do not silence every error
content.text: A broad `except Exception: pass` can hide real problems. Catch the specific error you expect and handle it deliberately.

content.question: Where is the actual error type usually shown in a traceback?
options: On the last line of the traceback
content.explanation: The final line names the exception and gives its message.

content.text: A virtual environment keeps a project's packages separate from the rest of your computer. It prevents version conflicts and makes a project reproducible.
Create one environment per project. Activate it before installing packages. Record dependencies in a requirements file so another machine can recreate the setup.

content.code:
# macOS / Linux
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install requests
pip freeze > requirements.txt

# Windows PowerShell
py -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pip install requests

rows: A folder containing a project-specific Python environment
A list of dependencies and versions
Tell the terminal to use the environment

content.title: Do not commit .venv
content.text: The environment can be large and machine-specific. Add `.venv/` to `.gitignore` and commit the requirements file instead.

content.question: Why use a virtual environment?
options: To keep dependencies isolated per project
content.explanation: Isolated environments prevent package version conflicts between projects.

modules.title: Build an expense tracker
modules.summary: A complete command-line project, from design to test.

content.text: Before writing code, decide what the program does, what data it stores, and how the user interacts with it.

Your expense tracker will add expenses, list them, show a total, filter by category, and save data to JSON. Keep the first version small; a clean core is easier to extend than a half-finished feature collection.

items: Define the data shape: a list of dictionaries with `amount`, `category`, `note`, and `date`.
Write the menu and the input loops.
Implement one feature at a time and test after each.
Separate data logic (load, save, add, total) from display logic.
Add error handling for bad numbers and missing files.
Only then add polish such as colours or summaries.

content.title: Write the smallest version that works
content.text: A tracker that can add and list one expense is already a program. Add features only after the current version runs and saves correctly.

content.question: Why separate data logic from display logic?
options: It makes the logic easier to test, reuse, and debug
content.explanation: Separating concerns lets you test calculations without depending on printed output.

content.text: Build a working command-line tracker in one file. The goal is clear behaviour and readable functions, not clever tricks.

content.title: What makes this a real program?
content.text: It persists data, validates input, handles an empty state, separates concerns, and has a clear entry point. Those habits matter more than the number of features.

content.question: Why use if __name__ == "__main__": in a script?
options: It makes the program run faster
It runs main() only when the file is executed directly, not when imported
content.explanation: This guard keeps the script reusable as a module without automatically launching the menu.

content.text: Testing is not a final ceremony. It is how you discover whether the program matches the story you told yourself.

Start with manual test cases: empty file, one expense, invalid amount, category filter with no matches, and a second run that loads existing data. Then move the pure logic into testable functions and use Python's `unittest` or `pytest` for repeatable checks.

content.title: Extension menu
content.text: Add monthly totals, a delete command, CSV export, a budget warning, or a simple chart with matplotlib. Choose one, write a test, implement it, and test again.
What to keep in your project folder

items: The Python source file.
A sample `expenses.json` or a note explaining how it is created.
A README with run instructions and example usage.
A `.gitignore` that excludes `.venv/` and personal data files.
Tests or a short manual test checklist.
A note about what you would build next.

content.question: What is a good first test for a file-backed program?
options: The empty state when no file exists
content.explanation: The empty state is a common failure point and a simple place to start.

finalAssessment.title: Python Pioneer assessment
finalAssessment.intro: Answer all eight questions. Score 80% or higher to earn the Python Pioneer badge and certificate.

questions.question: What does input() return?
questions.explanation: User input is read as text and must be converted for numeric work.

questions.question: How many values does range(1, 5) produce?
questions.explanation: It produces 1, 2, 3, 4. The stop value is excluded.

questions.question: What does return do?
options: Sends a value back to the caller
questions.explanation: Return ends the function and passes a value back.

questions.question: What is tasks[-1]?
questions.explanation: Negative indexes count backwards from the end of the list.

questions.question: Which file mode erases existing contents when opened?
questions.explanation: Write mode truncates the file when opened.

questions.question: What is the safest pattern for closing a file?
questions.explanation: The with statement closes the file automatically, even if an error occurs.

questions.question: Why use if __name__ == "__main__":?
options: To run main() only when the file is executed directly
questions.explanation: It prevents the main program from running when the file is imported as a module.
